Empirical Research Plan ‑ “Sin Stock Shunning and its Consequences”

------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
------------------------------------------------------------
Primary design: Difference-in-Differences (DID) with an event-study extension.

Why DID?  
• A large, plausibly exogenous shock to social attitudes toward one subset of vice products occurs in 1964-65: the U.S. Surgeon General’s Report (Jan-1964) and the Federal Cigarette Labeling and Advertising Act (July-1965).  
• Only tobacco producers (“Tobacco” = FF 5 “Smoke”) experience a discrete jump in stigma at that moment; alcohol & gaming were already stigmatized and did not face a comparable incremental shift.  
• We observe long firm-level panels (ownership 1980-2003, coverage 1976-2003, valuations 1965-2004, returns monthly 1926-2004, etc.) allowing pre-/post- shock comparison.  

Thus we can compare:  
(1) Treated firms = tobacco producers  
(2) Control firms = alcohol & gaming producers (already “vice” but no new shock) AND a second matched set of non-vice consumer discretionary firms (exact matches on size & industry to assure robustness).  

Specification:  
Outcome_it = α_i + γ_t + β·(Tobacco_i × Post1965_t) + δX_it + ε_it  

• β captures incremental effect of the post-1965 stigma jump on treated firms relative to their counterfactual.  
• We will also estimate an event-study allowing year-specific coefficients to inspect dynamic parallel trends.  
• For outcomes driven by investor clientele (institutional ownership by type, analyst coverage) we add a triple-difference (DDD): constrained vs unconstrained owner types.  

------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
• Tobacco_i = 1 if firm’s primary FF industry = Smoke (or if ≥50 % of segment sales from smoke, using Compustat Segments).  
• Post1965_t = 1 for fiscal years (or months) whose fiscal year-end is 1965 or later.

Control groups  
A. “Within-sin” control: FF 4 Beer & NAICS gaming companies.  
B. Matched “non-sin” control: Consumer nondurables firms matched 1:3 by pre-1964 size & book-to-market.  

Treatment timing  
• Event year = 1965 (report+law) with −5 to +10 yrs windows; robustness uses 1964 or 1966 cutoffs.  

------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends – Absent the Surgeon General shock, tobacco outcomes would have continued to evolve like those of control groups.  
• Plausibility: Alcohol & gaming face similar regulation, demand cyclicality, and capital-market access; pre-1964 series should be parallel.  
• Test: Plot pre-trend coefficients; run placebo cutoffs in 1958-63.

A2. No simultaneous shocks differentially hitting treatment.  
• Discussion: 1950s antitrust suits and 1990s state settlements are outside (+30 yrs), but we must rule out e.g., excise-tax changes in 1965. Control by adding year FE and macro controls.

A3. Stable composition – Entry/exit unrelated to treatment.  
• Check attrition; re-weight by inverse probability of survival; run balanced-panel robustness.

A4. Consistent classification – Firms do not switch industry classification endogenously because of the shock.  
• Verify using segment-level sales; exclude diversified conglomerates.

------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats & Mitigation
------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Regulatory / litigation events contemporaneous with stigma shock (e.g., 1965 labeling act may impose direct costs).  
→ Include policy controls (excise taxes, marketing restrictions); implement “net-of-cost” outcomes (e.g., abnormal returns controlling for estimated cash-flow impact).  

T2. Differential demand shocks (e.g., health concerns reducing cigarette sales).  
→ Include firm sales growth as control; show results for ownership/coverage (purely capital-market variables) where product demand changes should not mechanically drive effects.  

T3. Pre-trend divergence (threat to parallel-trend).  
→ Event-study plot with 5 pre-years; run falsification using alcohol prohibition repeal in 1933 on current sin firms as placebo.  

------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
------------------------------------------------------------
```r
#-------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
#-------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # fast high-dim FE regressions
library(ggplot2)

#-------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load & merge data
#-------------------------------------------------
crsp    <- fread("crsp_monthly.csv")        # permno, date, ret, prc, shrout
comp    <- fread("compustat_annual.csv")    # gvkey, fyear, at, sale, lt, ...
segments<- fread("compustat_segments.csv")  # gvkey, fyear, segment_sales, naics
ibes    <- fread("ibes_analyst.csv")        # ticker, fyear, n_analysts
cdr13f  <- fread("institutional_ownership.csv") # cusip, fyear, inst_type, shares
ff_ind  <- fread("ff48_industry_class.csv") # permno, ff48

# merge example: firm-year panel
panel <- merge(comp, ff_ind, by = c("permno","fyear"))
panel <- merge(panel, ibes,   by = c("permno","fyear"), all.x = TRUE)
panel <- merge(panel, cdr13f, by = c("permno","fyear"), all.x = TRUE)

#-------------------------------------------------
# 2. Construct treatment & covariates
#-------------------------------------------------
panel[, tobacco := as.integer(ff48 == 5)]                 # Smoke
panel[, alcohol := as.integer(ff48 == 4)]
panel[, gaming  := as.integer(naics %in% c(713210,713290))]

panel[, post65  := as.integer(fyear >= 1965)]
panel[, treat   := tobacco * post65]

# outcome examples
panel[, inst_bank_share := shares_bank / shares_outstanding]
panel[, analyst_coverage := fifelse(is.na(n_analysts),0,n_analysts)]
panel[, bm := book_equity / mkt_cap]

#-------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main DID regression: Institutional ownership
#-------------------------------------------------
did1 <- feols(inst_bank_share ~ treat + tobacco + post65 + size + bm |
              permno + fyear, data = panel)
summary(did1)

# Event-study
panel[, rel_year := fyear - 1965]
est <- feols(inst_bank_share ~ i(rel_year, tobacco, ref = -1) + size + bm |
             permno + fyear, data = panel[rel_year >= -5 & rel_year <= 10])
iplot(est)

#-------------------------------------------------
# 4. Robustness: Matched non-sin control sample
#-------------------------------------------------
# Propensity score match pre-1964
pre <- panel[fyear < 1964]
pre[, ps := glm(tobacco ~ log(at) + bm, family = binomial, data = pre)$fitted]
# nearest-neighbor
library(MatchIt)
m.out <- matchit(tobacco ~ log(at) + bm, data = pre, method = "nearest", ratio = 3)
matched_ids <- get_matches(m.out)$permno
panel_matched <- panel[permno %in% c(pre[tobacco==1]$permno, matched_ids)]

did2 <- feols(inst_bank_share ~ treat + size + bm |
              permno + fyear, data = panel_matched)
summary(did2)
```

------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
------------------------------------------------------------
Theory: If norm-constrained investors avoid newly stigmatised tobacco stocks, we expect:

• Institutional ownership by norm-sensitive types (banks, insurance, pensions) to fall 3-7 p.p. relative to control firms.  
• Analyst coverage to decline by ~1 analyst on a base of 5-6.  
• Valuations (price-to-book) to drop by 0.2–0.4 relative to matched peers, raising expected returns by ~30-50 bp/month (≈4–6 % p.a.).  
• Capital structure: higher leverage (1–1.5 turns more market-value leverage) as external equity becomes costlier.

------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)
------------------------------------------------------------
C1 Parallel pre-trends visually verified ............ 1  
C2 No other major shocks at event date .............. 0.5 (some regulation risk)  
C3 Stable composition / no endogenous switching ..... 0.5  
C4 No differential measurement error ................ 1  
C5 SUTVA – no spillovers between firms .............. 0.5 (some portfolio-rebalancing spillovers possible)

Overall score = 3.5 / 5.
